title: Conquering Italy
objective: After this level you can explain how Rome came to control the Italian peninsula, and the role of roads and alliances.
summary: Rome beat the Samnites, built the Via Appia from 312 BCE and made defeated peoples allies. By about 264 BCE it controlled Italy.

cards.headline: Rome won Italy with armies, roads and allies.
cards.body: Swords can win land. Roads and allies help you keep it.

cards.headline: Wars in the hills
cards.body: From 343 to 290 BCE, Rome fought the Samnite Wars against the hill peoples of central and southern Italy, a struggle for control of the peninsula. Rome came out on top. By about 264 BCE it controlled nearly all of Italy south of the Po Valley. The little town on the Tiber now ran almost the whole boot, minus the top.

cards.headline: Roads and allies
cards.body: In 312 BCE Rome began the Via Appia, its first great road, built to move armies quickly to the south. But the smarter move was what Rome did with the people it beat. Defeated Italian peoples became allies who supplied soldiers instead of paying tribute, and some were granted citizenship. So every war Rome won made its next army bigger. Lose to Rome, and you ended up marching for it.

cards.fact: A victory that cost too much.
cards.context: King Pyrrhus of Epirus beat Roman armies, but at such a cost that his name became a warning. A “Pyrrhic victory” now means a win that costs too much.

cards.headline: Italy: united
learned: Rome fought the Samnite Wars, 343–290 BCE
The Via Appia was begun in 312 BCE
By about 264 BCE Rome controlled Italy

questions.explanation: Begun in 312 BCE, the Via Appia was Rome’s first great road, built to move armies south.

questions.prompt: How did Rome keep conquered Italian peoples loyal?

options.label: It made them allies who supplied soldiers
It forced them all to move to Rome
It let each city choose a king

questions.explanation: Defeated peoples became allies who sent soldiers rather than tribute, and some gained citizenship.

questions.prompt: From Level 12: which Roman officials led the armies in these wars?
questions.explanation: Consuls commanded Rome’s armies, including in the wars that won Italy.
